concerns.question: The three Boolean facts express the listed classifications, but supply no additional conditions that could distinguish a necessary threshold from a sufficient licensing trigger. This is a missing substantive rule, not a reason to invent another fact.

“That business” in hong_kong refers back to the business described in business. The vocabulary does not specify how to classify hong_kong when no such business exists; unknown inputs must not silently become false.
Case-specific business classification, the ordinary-course qualification and incorporated authority remain outside these predicates. Their resolution cannot be inferred from the fact names.
Does “must be present in order to give rise to” specify the complete selected trigger, or only a necessary condition for a licensing obligation?
Should the contextual emphasis on carrying on a business qualify the express “at least one” threshold? The supplied text does not conclusively reconcile them.

The three Boolean facts express alternative connective structures, but cannot express whether the stated threshold is merely necessary or legally sufficient. A necessary-only interpretation leaves the actual trigger underdetermined.

“That business” makes hong_kong dependent on identifying the relevant business. The vocabulary supplies no rule for an absent business or unknown location; neither should silently be assigned a truth value.

The case-specific business classification, ordinary-course qualification, regulatory intent and incorporated authority cannot be independently represented by these three facts. They remain external qualifications rather than additional encoded exceptions.

Does “must be present in order to give rise to” state only a necessary threshold, or is the sentence intended to specify a sufficient trigger? On the necessary-only reading, the three facts can establish the threshold but cannot establish that a licensing obligation arises.

Can the missing Circular or incorporated Ordinance resolve the tension between the express “at least one” threshold and the surrounding discussion of carrying on a business? Their contents are not supplied.

The supplied Boolean facts describe classifications, not the modal relation between a necessary condition and a sufficient licensing trigger. No additional opaque legal-judgment fact should substitute for the missing substantive rule.

“That business” presupposes identification of the business referenced by business. The vocabulary does not specify the value of hong_kong when that business is absent or unidentified; unknown inputs must remain unknown.

The case-specific classification factors and ordinary-course qualification in Q3 cannot be represented independently using the fixed vocabulary. They may inform business externally, but business being false cannot automatically be treated as an independent exemption under the OR reading.
The Circular and incorporated Ordinance are not supplied. Their content, regulatory intent and any independent qualifications cannot be inferred from the fact names or the source URL.

No additional substantive parse absent from the prior hypotheses is supported by the supplied text. Does the selected experiment treat the express threshold as the complete antecedent, or require a sufficient licensing trigger that the necessary-condition wording leaves unspecified?

The prior cumulative reading remains a contextual possibility, but the enumerative “and” does not itself override “at least one”. Does the missing Circular or incorporated Ordinance establish a cumulative requirement?
Does the ordinary-course language merely guide classification of business, or independently qualify application of the licensing trigger? The supplied text does not settle that distinction.
